title: One Small Word Steals the Victory Speech
summary: From Michigan to the Middle East, many Arabs are celebrating Abdul El-Sayed's Senate victory — and one small word from his victory speech. El-Sayed, the son of Egyptian immigrants, won a Senate seat in Michigan and will be the first Muslim American U.S. senator. At his Election Night rally in Detroit on November 4, he opened with a playful greeting for Vice President JD Vance: 'JD, habibi.' Vance had warned during the campaign that El-Sayed would lead rioters in burning down Detroit. El-Sayed noted the irony that Vance is constitutionally obligated to swear him in as a senator in January. 'Habibi' literally means 'my beloved' in Arabic, and it shows up often in Arab pop songs. In everyday speech, it usually means something closer to 'buddy,' 'pal,' or 'bro.' El-Sayed's supporters wore shirts reading 'Habibi for Abdul.' In his speech, El-Sayed also said his campaign had turned 'inshallah,' meaning 'God willing,' into 'hamdulillah,' meaning 'thank God.' The lighthearted moment struck a chord. People shared music video clips featuring the word 'habibi' on social media, and one user joked that a song by Egyptian singer Shireen Abd El-Wahab could become the new national anthem. Egyptian academic Khalil al-Anani called 'habibi' the sweetest word and thanked the senator-elect for bringing joy to Egyptians. Egyptians are known across the Arab world for their sense of humor, often joking even in hard times. The celebration stood out in a region shaped by past and present conflicts, which have also fed negative stereotypes about Arabs in the West. El-Sayed faced harsh rhetoric during the campaign. President Donald Trump called him a 'jihadist,' brought up the September 11 attacks, and repeatedly misstated his name. In his speech, El-Sayed answered with a joke of his own, telling Trump that after Vance swears him in, the president can simply call him 'senator.'
why_it_matters: The moment shows how a single word can push back against negative stereotypes about Arabs and turn harsh campaign rhetoric into shared laughter. It also matters because El-Sayed will be the first Muslim American U.S. senator, so his victory is a milestone for representation.
